title: Chimpay to the Tiber: the Cacique's Son, the Salesian Bargain, and the Body That Came Back Twice
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Salt Country and the Line of Calfucurá

stops.name: Araucanía, the llaimache country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no register survives, and the year is counted backward from the age of ninety-seven given at his death in 1908; the coordinate marks the Araucanian country of the lineage, not a documented birthplace
stops.campa: Manuel Namuncurá is born on the Chilean side of the cordillera, among the llaimache, son of Juan Calfucurá. No parish book holds the day. The year is arithmetic, subtracted from an old man's reported age at his death. West of the Andes the family are Araucanians under no state at all; east of them lies a salt country his father intends to rule. He will cross that range once, in one direction, and never live west of it again. His own son, born seventy-five years after him on the far side of the pampa, will die in Rome.
suggested_refs: The Araucanía of the llaimache lineage, west of the Andes, before the crossing of 1831

stops.name: Salinas Grandes, the crossing east
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only in es.wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Calfucurá brings the llaimache over the cordillera and down onto the salitral, and there builds the confederation of Salinas Grandes: a state of tents astride the salt roads, treating with Buenos Aires as one power treats with another. Juan Manuel de Rosas, whose own desert campaign will cross this same country three years later, is the man Calfucurá names as the authority that sent him. The claim is made thirty years afterward, to a Chilean who writes it down. Manuel is twenty and rides in the column, learning the ground his son will be born on.
stops.quote: Yo soy chileno, me vine a estas tierras por orden de don Juan Manuel Rosas
stops.quote_source: Juan Calfucurá, 27 April 1861, as reported in El Mercurio (Santiago), 'La sangre chilena del nuevo beato mapuche argentino,' 18 November 2007; a newspaper's report of an utterance made 146 years earlier, with no archival document behind it
suggested_refs: The salitral of Salinas Grandes, seat of the Calfucurá confederation
sources: El Mercurio, 18 November 2007 (Wayback snapshot of mapuche.info/news/merc071118.html)

stops.name: Paraná, the font and the constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month and day defaulted to 01, and the church is not named in the source
stops.campa: In the capital of the Confederation the cacique's son is baptized and takes the name Manuel. Justo José de Urquiza, who governs the country from this city, stands as his godfather, and Manuel swears loyalty to the constitution sworn the year before. He goes back to Salinas Grandes with a Christian name and a set of papers, and nothing about his authority over the tolderías changes. Forty-three years later he will hand a son of his own to a priest, and that boy will not come back. The oath costs him nothing on the day he swears it.
suggested_refs: The city of Paraná, capital of the Argentine Confederation, 1854

stops.name: Salinas Grandes, the inheritance and the rivals
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia dates Calfucurá's death to June 1873 and the consolidation of Manuel's authority to 1875
stops.campa: Calfucurá dies and the confederation does not pass whole. Manuel takes the cacicazgo against his brother José Millaqueucurá and his cousin Bernardo Namuncurá, and two years pass before the tolderías answer to one man again. He inherits a machine his father built for a frontier that is closing: five thousand lances, the salt roads, the treaties, the tribute. Buenos Aires has just begun to think of the pampa as unfinished national territory rather than as a border. Manuel is the last man to command it as a country of his own.
suggested_refs: The succession of 1873-1875 in the Salinas Grandes confederation

stops.name: The pampa frontier, the price of not invading
stops.date_confidence: contested: the source places the demands before the newly installed government of Nicolás Avellaneda, who took office 12 October 1874; es.wikipedia's 'end of 1875' belongs to a different sentence. Month defaulted to 12, day to 01
stops.campa: To the government just installed in Buenos Aires, Manuel Namuncurá sends terms. Forty thousand gold pesos, four thousand six hundred cows, six thousand mares, a hundred working oxen, silk cloth, tobacco, wine, arms, four general's uniforms. He offers besides to sell his war captives at forty gold pesos a head. The list ends with soap, which the source sets down outside the quoted demands. The government of Nicolás Avellaneda reads the paper as extortion. Manuel is pricing a peace he can still withhold, and the price is refused.
stops.quote: Cuarenta mil pesos oro, cuatro mil seiscientas vacas, seis mil yeguas, cien bueyes para trabajar, telas de seda, tabaco, vino, armas, cuatro uniformes de general, etc.
stops.quote_source: Manuel Namuncurá's terms to the Avellaneda government, as given on the Instituto Malvinas page 'Manuel Namuncura (Pie de Piedra)' (Wayback snapshot); the soap appears in the page's own following sentence, outside the quotation marks, and is not part of the quoted list
suggested_refs: The Instituto Malvinas transcription of Namuncurá's peace terms, an amateur page offering no archival citation
sources: Instituto Malvinas, 'Manuel Namuncura (Pie de Piedra)' (Wayback snapshot)

stops.name: Azul, the malón of 1875
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; sources give the strength as 3,500 to 4,000 (es.wikipedia, 'Manuel Namuncurá') and as 5,000 (es.wikipedia, 'Conquista del Desierto'), a discrepancy left open here
stops.campa: The terms are refused, and Namuncurá rides. With Juan José Catriel, with Pincén, with Baigorrita, he throws somewhere between three and a half and five thousand lances against Tres Arroyos, Tandil and Azul, and comes back with cattle and captives across a frontier line that has just shown it cannot hold. It is the largest indigenous offensive the province has seen and the last of its size. In Buenos Aires it ends a decade-old argument about whether the desert should be fenced or taken.
suggested_refs: The great malón of 1875 against Tres Arroyos, Tandil and Azul

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Roca writes to the president
stops.date_confidence: attested: the letter is dated, and reproduced in Juan Carlos Walther, La conquista del desierto (Eudeba, 1970), p. 239
stops.campa: Six months after the malón a colonel who is not yet minister of war writes to Nicolás Avellaneda with a plan. Extinguish them, or throw them across the Río Negro; Rosas nearly finished the work already. Julio Argentino Roca sets down in a private letter the policy the republic will execute within four years against the confederation Namuncurá commands. He writes it as a comparison of methods and their costs. The boy who will be carried to Rome is not born for another eleven years.
stops.quote: A mi juicio, el mejor sistema para concluir con los indios, ya sea extinguiéndolos o arrojándolos al otro lado del río Negro, es el de la guerra ofensiva que fue seguida por Rosas que casi concluyó con ellos...
stops.quote_source: Julio Argentino Roca to President Nicolás Avellaneda, 19 October 1875, quoted in Juan Carlos Walther, La conquista del desierto (Buenos Aires: Eudeba, 1970), p. 239
suggested_refs: Roca's 1875 letter to Avellaneda, the earliest written statement of the campaign's logic
sources: Walther, La conquista del desierto (1970), p. 239

stops.name: Salinas Grandes, the tolderías abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only in es.wikipedia, 'Conquista del Desierto'; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Columns under Nicolás Levalle and Marcelino Freyre come onto the salt flats and kill more than two hundred of Namuncurá's warriors. He leaves the tolderías standing and goes west with what will follow him. The confederation's capital, the salt, the treaty ground, the graves of Calfucurá's people: all of it is given up in a season, not stormed. Roca has been arguing for years that a ditch cannot hold a frontier and that only occupation can. The salt flats prove him right in the same year his column reaches the Río Negro.
suggested_refs: The 1879 operations of Levalle and Freyre against the Salinas Grandes tolderías

stops.name: Choele Choel, the column on the Río Negro
stops.date_confidence: attested: dated in julio_argentino_roca.journey.json from the campaign record
stops.campa: Roca's column reaches the island country of Choele Choel and camps on the Río Negro, and the desert is declared finished. The Mapuche and Ranquel nations, their herds, their salt roads and their long treaties are written up as cleared ground. Namuncurá is somewhere west with the remainder of his people, not yet surrendered, no longer a power. Seven years from now and a day's ride upriver, a sixth child will be born to him in a village on this same bank. The republic will have reached it first.
stops.quote: ¡Qué disparate la zanja de Alsina! Y Avellaneda lo deja hacer. Es lo que se le ocurre a un pueblo débil y en la infancia: atajar con murallas a sus enemigos.
stops.quote_source: Julio Argentino Roca on Adolfo Alsina's defensive ditch, quoted in Leopoldo Lugones, Roca (Buenos Aires: Comisión Nacional del Monumento al Teniente General Julio A. Roca, 1938), p. 176; the remark is undated in the source
suggested_refs: Roca's camp at Choele Choel, June 1879

stops.name: Fisque Menuco, the fort in the valley
stops.date_confidence: attested: dated in julio_argentino_roca.journey.json
stops.campa: The column names a fort in the upper valley of the Río Negro at Fisque Menuco, and the fort will take the general's name and keep it. Fewer than a hundred kilometres downriver lies the stretch of bank where Chimpay will stand. The corridor Roca garrisons in June 1879 is the exact corridor in which Ceferino Namuncurá will be born, baptized, and finally beatified. Roca does not know the child's name. He is drawing the map the child's life will be lived on, seven years before the child is born.
suggested_refs: The fort at Fisque Menuco, later General Roca, Río Negro

stops.name: Ñorquín, the surrender
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia, 'Manuel Namuncurá'; the coordinate is the departmental centre at El Huecú, not a pinpointed campsite
stops.campa: After five years of moving ahead of the army through Neuquén, Manuel Namuncurá comes in at Ñorquín with about three hundred warriors, hungry and without weapons. He is the last cacique general of Salinas Grandes and he surrenders what is left of it in one morning. Campaigning against other groups continues in the cordillera after this date; what ends here is the confederation. He is roughly seventy-three years old. He has spent fifty-three years east of the Andes and now signs the country away in the foothills of the range he crossed as a boy.
suggested_refs: The surrender at Ñorquín, 21 March 1884

stops.name: Bahía Blanca, the march in to the port
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: From Ñorquín the column of the surrendered is walked east to Bahía Blanca to formalize submission before military authority. The road runs back across the salitral he governed, past the abandoned tolderías, to a port town built on the frontier that his lances used to cross at will. The salt flats he crosses as a prisoner of the state are the ones his father crossed as a conqueror in 1831. Fifty-three years lie between the two crossings, and the same ground is under both.
suggested_refs: The port of Bahía Blanca, mustering point for the surrendered tolderías, June 1884

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the steamship Pomona
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month only in es.wikipedia; the day 15 is a placeholder within June 1884 and should not be read as documented
stops.campa: The steamship Pomona carries Manuel Namuncurá up to Buenos Aires, and the capital receives the cacique it has spent a decade describing as the desert itself. Roca has been president of this country since 1880 and governs the apparatus, church and army together, into which the surrendered are now to be fitted. Namuncurá is not jailed but entertained, photographed and enrolled. He will come back to petition this city in 1886, in 1894, and again in 1897, and a cacique who petitions costs the state less than a cacique who raids.
suggested_refs: The steamship Pomona, which carried Namuncurá to Buenos Aires in June 1884

stops.name: San Ignacio, the colony and the colonelcy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month and day defaulted to 01, though the grant follows the June visit. The coordinate for San Ignacio is approximate; sources place it about 60 km from Junín de los Andes
stops.campa: The republic gives Manuel Namuncurá land at the indigenous colony of San Ignacio in Neuquén and the honorary rank of colonel in the army that beat him. Both are policy. A surrendered cacique drawing an officer's pay stops being a frontier and becomes an administrative unit. He accepts both. The colony sits in the cordillera country, far from the salt flats he governed, and he will live twenty-four more years on it. It is here, eventually, that his son's bones will be brought to lie under a mound shaped like a drum.
suggested_refs: The San Ignacio indigenous colony, Neuquén, granted to Namuncurá after the surrender

stops.name: Chimpay, the sixth child
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in both the English and Spanish Wikipedia articles
stops.campa: Ceferino Namuncurá is born on the bank of the Río Negro at Chimpay, sixth child of the colonel-cacique and of Rosario Burgos. What Burgos was is not settled: a Chilean mestiza in one account, a Chilean captive in another, and in the scholarly literature simply his mother, without qualifier. The village sits inside the corridor Roca's column garrisoned seven years before. The boy is born a subject of the state that took the pampa from his grandfather, on the river that was drawn as the line the desert would be pushed behind.
stops.quote: Según cuenta la historia, Ceferino fue hijo de la mestiza chilena Rosario Burgos, pero hasta el momento se habría indicado, equivocadamente, que su padre, Manuel Namuncurá, tendría sangre argentina.
stops.quote_source: El Mercurio (Santiago), 'La sangre chilena del nuevo beato mapuche argentino,' 18 November 2007; es.wikipedia's body text calls Burgos a captive rather than a mestiza, and María Andrea Nicoletti names her without either qualifier
suggested_refs: The birth house at Chimpay, on the Río Negro

stops.name: The Río Negro bank, the child in the water
stops.date_confidence: tradition: the near-drowning is carried by en.wikipedia as legend, with no date, place or circumstance documented; the year and the coordinate are both placeholders
stops.campa: The story the Patagonian devotion tells first is water. The child falls into the Río Negro and is pulled out alive, and the river that gave the campaign its name and the province its name gives him back. No document holds the episode. The tradition names no year, no witness and no circumstance, and the pin here is a placeholder. It is told at Chimpay before he is famous and it is still told there, at the same bend, by people who bring their own children to the water.
suggested_refs: The bend of the Río Negro at Chimpay, site of the near-drowning tradition

stops.name: Chimpay, the Salesian at the font
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia gives 24 December 1887, en.wikipedia says he was baptized at age eight by the same priest, which would place it around 1894; the two are not reconcilable and are not resolved here
stops.campa: Domingo Milanesio, the Salesian missionary who works the Río Negro after the army, baptizes Ceferino Namuncurá. Whether the boy is one year old or eight depends on which encyclopaedia is open. The order that reaches Chimpay in the wake of the columns is the same order that will school him, ship him to Italy, bury him in Rome, and spend the next century pressing his cause at the Vatican. His father was baptized himself at forty-three, with the head of the Confederation standing as godfather.
suggested_refs: The Salesian mission of Domingo Milanesio on the Río Negro

stops.name: La Boca, the carpenter's apprentice
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: en.wikipedia attests the apprenticeship at the National Workshops of the Navy without a date or a site; the year and the Riachuelo waterfront coordinate are both inferred, and the earlier research pool placed this pin on the Casa Rosada in error
stops.campa: Sent ahead of his schooling, Ceferino spends a stretch at the Talleres Nacionales de Marina learning carpentry. It is the ordinary destination for an indigenous boy in the capital in the 1890s: a trade, a workshop on the Riachuelo, a wage. He does not stay. His father pulls him out and hands him to the priests instead. The English article attests the apprenticeship and gives it neither a date nor an address, so the year and the waterfront here are both inferred. Where the boy stood with a plane in his hands is not recorded anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The Talleres Nacionales de Marina on the Riachuelo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Almagro, the Colegio Pío IX
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the Salesian complex at Hipólito Yrigoyen 4085, Almagro, corrected from a pin that had fallen 1.6 km west near Caballito
stops.campa: Manuel Namuncurá delivers his son to the Salesians as a boarder at the Colegio Pío IX. The historians read the act as a calculation rather than a conversion: the missionaries have the ear of the state, and a cacique with a son inside their house has a claim on both. No document survives in which Manuel says so. The reading is the consensus of the literature and nothing more. Both encyclopaedias give the day. The boy is eleven and enters as an ordinary interno.
suggested_refs: The Salesian complex of the Colegio Pío IX and the Basílica de María Auxiliadora y San Carlos, Almagro

stops.name: Almagro, the first communion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia
stops.campa: A year into the school Ceferino makes his first communion in the parish church attached to it. The Salesians keep a record of him from this point that is unusually full for a boy of twelve, and it is kept because of who his father is. The order understands the value of the pupil it has: proof, in a single body, that the desert can be brought inside the Church. Almost everything known about his boyhood survives because the order had that reason to write it down.
suggested_refs: The parish of San Carlos, adjoining the Colegio Pío IX

stops.name: Almagro, the confirmation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia
stops.campa: Bishop Gregorio Romero confirms him at San Carlos, beside the college. He is thirteen. In Neuquén his father is a colonel on paper with a colony to feed and a standing petition in Buenos Aires; in Almagro his son is being moved through the sacraments one at a time, on the order's schedule. What the boy makes of it is not recorded anywhere. The register holds a name, a date and a bishop's signature, and that is the whole of the evidence for this year of his life.
suggested_refs: The confirmation register of the parish of San Carlos, Almagro

stops.name: Almagro, the prince of Christian doctrine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2 April 1901 academy entry in en.wikipedia; the 'Prince of Christian Doctrine' distinction is dated only to around 1900, and the presence of Carlos Gardel in the same school rests on the contested francesista account of his birth
stops.campa: The school gives him a title, Prince of Christian Doctrine, for knowing the catechism better than anyone in the house. Buenos Aires later adds a second boy to the same corridor: Carlos Gardel, who according to one half of a still unsettled argument about his birth was a boarder here in 1901 and 1902, and according to the other half was in Montevideo. The Italian encyclopaedia does not mention him at all. What the English record supports is narrower: Ceferino enters the school's academy on 2 April 1901.
suggested_refs: The disputed Pío IX schooling of Carlos Gardel, francesista versus uruguayista

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; en.wikipedia says early 1902, no site is named, and the coordinate marks central Buenos Aires
stops.campa: The doctors name it: tuberculosis of the lung. He is fifteen and has spent five years in the damp of the port city, in dormitories, in a climate his body has no history with. The disease that will kill him arrives with the education his father bought him. No source names the doctor, the hospital or the month. From this year forward every move he makes is prescribed by his lungs. Viedma, Turin, Frascati, the island in the Tiber: all of it is treatment, and all of it fails.
suggested_refs: The 1902 tuberculosis diagnosis, unlocated in the sources

stops.name: Viedma, the college on the Río Negro
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month in es.wikipedia; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He is sent back down his own river to the Salesian college of San Francisco de Sales at Viedma, for the air and a lighter course of study, and enrolled as an aspirant to the seminary. He is in Patagonia again, at the river's mouth, four hundred kilometres from Chimpay and from the family that has not seen him in six years. He is not sent home. The order moves him within itself, from one of its houses to another, and no source records his family being asked.
suggested_refs: The Colegio San Francisco de Sales, Viedma

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the embarkation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the departure; neither the dock nor the ship is named in any source consulted
stops.campa: Archbishop Giovanni Cagliero, who has spent thirty years building the Salesian mission in Patagonia, takes the seventeen-year-old aboard for Italy. The reason given is his health, and Italian air, and continued formation. The reason that also holds is that the order is carrying its best argument to Rome in person. Nobody aboard records the departure as a last one. He sails out of the estuary of the Plata with tubercular lungs, in July, for a northern summer.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires dársena, point of departure on 19 July 1904

stops.name: Genoa, the probable landfall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no biographical source consulted names the Italian port of arrival. Genoa is the standard 1904 landfall for Salesian traffic between the Plata and Turin, and the date is inferred from a crossing of roughly three weeks
stops.campa: The Buenos Aires to Italy run comes in at Genoa, and from Genoa the Salesian road goes north to Turin. No source consulted says so of this crossing. It is the shape of the traffic in 1904 and nothing more, and it is entered here as a reconstruction rather than as a landing. What is certain is that he left the Plata on 19 July and was in Piedmont by August, and that between those two facts lies an unrecorded three weeks of Atlantic in which a boy with a wasting lung disease was a passenger.
suggested_refs: The Genoa to Turin route of Salesian traffic from the River Plate, 1904
sources: Reconstruction from standard 1904 steamer routes; no source names the arrival port

stops.name: Turin, the house at Valdocco
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by inference from the 19 July departure; the research pool had erroneously assigned the departure date 19 July 1904 to the Turin arrival as well. Day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Cagliero brings him to Valdocco, the founding house of the order, where Don Bosco is buried and where every Salesian in the world is from. The Patagonian boy walks into the room the Patagonian mission was invented in. He visits the tomb, according to the devotional accounts, though the scholarly ones do not carry it. He is a curiosity in Turin. The order that shows him to its own people is showing them what four decades of mission money produced, standing up and breathing badly.
suggested_refs: The Salesian motherhouse and Basilica of Mary Help of Christians at Valdocco, Turin
sources: corazones.org, biography of Ceferino Namuncurá (Don Bosco's tomb, devotional source)

stops.name: Rome, the audience with Pius X
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia and corazones.org; en.wikipedia gives only September 1904
stops.campa: Pius X receives him in the Apostolic Palace, and Ceferino Namuncurá gives the pope a Mapuche poncho. The grandson of Calfucurá, twenty years after Ñorquín, hands woven cloth to the bishop of Rome in a room built by the Renaissance. The boy is eighteen. The poncho comes from a country that was extinguished as a polity within his father's lifetime, and the exchange will be printed in Salesian bulletins in four languages. The Spanish sources date the audience to the day; the English one gives only the month.
suggested_refs: The Mapuche poncho presented to Pius X, September 1904

stops.name: Frascati, Villa Sora
stops.date_confidence: attested to the autumn of 1904; the month is inferred, the day defaulted to 01, and the coordinate marks the town of Frascati rather than the villa itself
stops.campa: He is moved out to the Salesian college of Villa Sora in the Alban hills, where the air is held to be better than Rome's. It is the third climate prescribed for him in two years and the last that will be tried. Frascati's slopes look down toward the city he has just left, vineyards and the ruins of old villas between the trees. He studies Latin there through a Roman winter, coughing the whole season, a Patagonian boy sent uphill for air that will not come. The hills do not work either.
suggested_refs: The Salesian college of Villa Sora, Frascati

stops.name: Isola Tiberina, the Fatebenefratelli
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1905 by the Spanish, English and Italian Wikipedia articles; the precise day of 28 March rests on corazones.org alone and is not used here. Day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The disease takes the upper hand and he is brought down into the city, to the hospital of the Fatebenefratelli on the island in the Tiber, a ward that has been treating the sick on that rock in one form or another since antiquity. José Lapponi, personal physician to Leo XIII and to Pius X, attends him. The Church gives its Patagonian aspirant the best medicine it owns. In 1905 nothing anyone owns cures pulmonary tuberculosis. Rest and air are the whole of the treatment, and he has been moved three times to get them.
suggested_refs: The Ospedale Fatebenefratelli, Isola Tiberina, Rome

stops.name: Isola Tiberina, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Spanish, English and Italian articles; corazones.org gives 11 November, which appears to confuse the date with the later beatification anniversary and is not followed here
stops.campa: Ceferino Namuncurá dies on an island in the Tiber, eighteen years old, eight months out of Argentina. Cagliero is with him. Most of his biographers give him the same last words, a blessing and a request to save his soul and let God's will do the rest. The same sentence also appears in his letters, and at least one historian holds that it was moved to the deathbed afterward to give the dying the shape the cause required. Both readings are printed. Neither has been withdrawn.
stops.quote: ¡Bendito sea Dios y María Santísima!; basta que pueda salvar mi alma y en los demás que se haga la santa voluntad de Dios.
stops.quote_source: Given as his last words by Néstor Noriega, Semblanza de Ceferino Namuncurá (Rosario: Didascalia, 2000), p. 26; the same prayer appears in his correspondence, Carta 37, in Luis Pedemonte, Cartas y escritos de Ceferino Namuncurá (Buenos Aires, 1949), p. 46. María Andrea Nicoletti, 'El camino a los altares,' Revista Tefros 7 (1-2), n. 50, argues it was relocated to the death scene. Neither the Noriega nor the Pedemonte page could be opened directly
suggested_refs: Noriega, Semblanza de Ceferino Namuncurá (2000), p. 26
Pedemonte, Cartas y escritos de Ceferino Namuncurá (1949), Carta 37

stops.name: Campo Verano, the wooden cross
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia; the plain wooden cross rests on that source alone, and the coordinate is corrected from a pin that fell outside the cemetery walls
stops.campa: He is buried the next day in the municipal cemetery of Rome, beside San Lorenzo fuori le Mura, under a wooden cross with his name on it. A few Salesians and a few fellow students attend. It is the burial the house gives a student who dies far from his family. The cacique's son is put into Italian ground in a common section with a zinc plate for identification, and it is that plate, nineteen years later, that will make it possible to say which bones in the row are his.
suggested_refs: The Cimitero del Verano, Rome, first burial place

stops.name: San Ignacio, the death of Manuel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia; the age of about 97 depends on the reconstructed birth year, and the coordinate for San Ignacio is approximate
stops.campa: Manuel Namuncurá dies at San Ignacio, about ninety-seven years old, three years after the son he sent to Rome. He has outlived the confederation, the war, the surrender, the colonelcy, and the boy. Where he is buried is not known. The last cacique general of Salinas Grandes has no located grave, and his son will be exhumed, catalogued, shipped across the Atlantic, moved twice more, and finally laid under a mound built in the shape of a ceremonial drum on the land the army gave the father.
suggested_refs: The lost grave of Manuel Namuncurá, San Ignacio, Neuquén

stops.name: Campo Verano, niche 358 opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; the exhumation record itself is undated in the reproduction consulted, and month and day are defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The grave is opened and the bones identified against the cemetery register, the zinc plate on the cross, and a second plate found among the remains. The act is written on parchment, signed, sealed in a glass tube with virgin wax, and put into the zinc urn with the bones, so that the next people to open it will know what they have. Roman bureaucracy performs, for a Mapuche seminarian dead of tuberculosis, the exact procedure it performs for a relic. The record assigns him niche 358, row 2.
stops.quote: Ceferino Namuncurá de 18 años, nacido en Chimpay Rio Negro y muerto el 11 de Mayo de 1905
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the identification plate found with the remains, quoted in the 1924 exhumation and identification record of the Cimitero Comunale Monumentale del Verano, Rome, as reproduced in es.wikipedia, 'Ceferino Namuncurá'; the record assigns the remains niche 358, row 2, new section
suggested_refs: The 1924 exhumation act of the Cimitero del Verano, niche 358, row 2
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Ceferino Namuncurá', section 'Traslado de sus restos'

stops.name: Fortín Mercedes, the chapel on the Colorado
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by both the English and Spanish articles; the month is a placeholder within 1924 and is not documented
stops.campa: Under the sponsorship of President Marcelo T. de Alvear the remains cross the Atlantic westward and are installed in the rebuilt chapel of an old frontier fort near Pedro Luro. Fortín Mercedes was a post of the line the Conquista del Desierto pushed south. The republic that took the pampa from Calfucurá brings Calfucurá's grandson home at state expense and lodges him in one of its own forts. Both encyclopaedias agree on the year of the repatriation and neither of them gives a day.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the old Fortín Mercedes, near Pedro Luro, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Rome, the cause opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia, which dates the opening of the cause to 2 May 1944; en.wikipedia gives 1945 for a petition presented to the Holy See. These are probably two procedural steps rather than a conflict, and are not merged here
stops.campa: Forty years after the death the Church opens the formal cause. The Salesians have kept the file warm since 1905 and the Patagonian devotion has never needed it: people have been praying to Ceferino Namuncurá without permission for four decades, at Fortín Mercedes and on the river bank at Chimpay. What opens in 1944 is the paperwork. It will run sixty-three more years and through six papacies before it closes, and it closes on the strength of one woman in Córdoba with a uterine tumour.
suggested_refs: The 2 May 1944 opening of the cause of beatification

stops.name: Rome, the witnesses and the writings
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia dates the gathering of testimony to 13 May to 10 July 1947 and the theological approval of his writings to 10 June 1949; the stop carries the earlier date
stops.campa: Between May and July the Church takes testimony from those still alive who knew him, and two years later his spiritual writings are approved as containing nothing contrary to doctrine. The letters of a Patagonian teenager are read line by line by Roman theologians. Among them is Carta 37, which carries the prayer that most of his biographers place on his deathbed instead. The file is now large enough to argue about, and the argument about where that sentence belongs starts inside it.
suggested_refs: The 1947 processo testimony and the 1949 approval of the writings

stops.name: Vatican City, Pius XII signs the introduction
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia; the research pool had misattributed this event to en.wikipedia and carried it as a bare year
stops.campa: Pius XII approves the formal introduction of the cause, which moves the case from an Argentine diocesan matter to a Roman one. Fifty-two years have passed since the boy died four kilometres from this desk. In Patagonia nothing changes: the pilgrimages to Fortín Mercedes and Chimpay have been running without Rome's approval since before the cause was opened, and they go on running through every further delay. The decree follows the devotion by half a century.
suggested_refs: The decree of 3 March 1957 introducing the cause

stops.name: Vatican City, declared venerable
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the superlative claim that he is the first Argentine and the first South American indigenous person so titled is as stated by en.wikipedia and has not been checked against a Vatican register
stops.campa: Paul VI declares Ceferino Namuncurá venerable, and the English source records the claim that he is the first Argentine and the first indigenous South American to hold the title. Heroic virtue is now official. What remains is a miracle, which is the one part of the process the Church cannot manufacture and must wait for. It waits twenty-eight years. During those years the relics stay at Fortín Mercedes and the buses keep coming down the Colorado to see them.
suggested_refs: The decree of venerability, 22 June 1972

stops.name: Fortín Mercedes, the relics into the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: contested: en.wikipedia dates the transfer to 1991 and es.wikipedia to 1992, a one-year discrepancy left open. Month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The relics are moved a short distance inside Fortín Mercedes, out of the chapel and into the larger sanctuary of María Auxiliadora, for security. The stated reason is the number of people arriving. Sixty-seven years after the repatriation the crowd has outgrown the room. The two encyclopaedias disagree by a year on when this happened and neither gives a day, which is the ordinary condition of the paperwork around a body that has now been moved four times and is not finished moving.
suggested_refs: The Santuario María Auxiliadora at Fortín Mercedes

stops.name: Córdoba, the woman with the tumours
stops.date_confidence: contested: en.wikipedia dates the confirmed recovery to 2000, while the Perfil interview of 2007 has Valeria Herrera diagnosed 'eight years ago,' around 1999; the Vatican's final ruling came in mid-2006. Month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Valeria Herrera of Córdoba, told her chances against uterine cancer are slight, prays to Ceferino Namuncurá over a weekend and returns to hospital on the Monday to find the tumours gone. Vatican-appointed pathologists examine the case and can offer no medical account of it. The final ruling comes in 2006. She is thirty-one when the beatification is announced, married, living in Alta Gracia, and unwilling to let the thing that happened to her be sold.
stops.quote: Tenía escasa posibilidad de cura según los médicos… En ese fin de semana recé y le pedí a Ceferino… El lunes cuando volví al hospital ya no había rastros de los tumores
stops.quote_source: Valeria Herrera, interviewed by Télam, in Diario Perfil (Buenos Aires), 11 November 2007 (Wayback snapshot); the article's headline, often quoted as her words, is a sub-editor's line and appears nowhere in her speech
suggested_refs: The Perfil interview with Valeria Herrera, 11 November 2007

stops.name: Chimpay, the Semana Ceferiniana
stops.date_confidence: attested: the forty thousand figure is for the 2006 feast, reported in Diario Río Negro, 26 August 2006, pp. 30-31, and cited by Nicoletti; the practice described is annual and continuing, so the stop sits at the last documented year before the beatification rather than at a single event
stops.campa: Every August, on his birthday rather than the day he died, Chimpay fills. Seven days of masses close with a concelebration by the bishops of Patagonia, mounted delegations ride in from the traditionalist centres of the region, and stalls sell along the route of the procession. Forty thousand people came in 2006, a year before Rome made anything official. Nicoletti calls him the popular saint of Patagonia, whose feast draws more of the faithful than any other in the region.
stops.quote: En la Patagonia Ceferino es el "santo popular" por excelencia, su festividad y su procesión religiosa es la que convoca más fieles en la región.
stops.quote_source: María Andrea Nicoletti, 'Ceferino Namuncurá: un indígena "virtuoso",' RUNA XXVII (2007), FFyL-UBA, pp. 121-145, body text; the attendance figure and the description of the Semana de la Fe appear in that article's footnote 10, citing Diario Río Negro, 26 August 2006
suggested_refs: Nicoletti, RUNA XXVII (2007), pp. 121-145, CONICET repository copy
Diario Río Negro, 'La gran fiesta de la Fe convocó a más de 40 mil personas en Chimpay,' 26 August 2006

stops.name: Vatican City, the decree of beatification
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia dates the decree 7 July 2007 and en.wikipedia 6 July 2007; the one-day discrepancy is not resolved here
stops.campa: Benedict XVI signs, and it is settled that the ceremony will not be held in Rome. The Church sends the beatification to Patagonia instead, to the village on the Río Negro, and sends Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone to preside as legate in the pope's place. A hundred and ten years after Manuel Namuncurá handed the boy to the Salesians in Almagro, and a hundred and two after the body was buried at the Verano, the Vatican decides that the proper place to raise him to the altars is the bank of the river he was pulled out of as a child.
suggested_refs: The beatification decree of July 2007

stops.name: Chimpay, the beatification
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the crowd is given as more than 100,000 by es.wikipedia and as more than 10,000 by en.wikipedia, an order-of-magnitude discrepancy left open
stops.campa: Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone proclaims him blessed in the open air at Chimpay, as papal legate. The Spanish account counts more than a hundred thousand people on the ground and the English account more than ten thousand, and no one reconciles them. Valeria Herrera is there. The grandson of the cacique who held the salt roads is beatified in a Patagonian village by an Italian cardinal, in front of a crowd nobody can count, on the river the army used as a line.
stops.quote: a mí se me dio la vida de nuevo, así que no puedo permitirme estar al servicio de la pavada
stops.quote_source: Valeria Herrera at Chimpay, on refusing commercial exploitation of the miracle, in Diario Perfil (Buenos Aires), 11 November 2007 (Wayback snapshot), sourced to Télam
suggested_refs: The open-air beatification Mass at Chimpay, 11 November 2007

stops.name: San Ignacio, the mound in the shape of a cultrún
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in es.wikipedia; that source places San Ignacio in Huiliches department, which cannot be right, since Huiliches has Junín de los Andes as its own capital and does not list San Ignacio among its communities, while the Aluminé department article does. Read as Aluminé, coordinate approximate
stops.campa: At the family's request the remains leave Fortín Mercedes for the last time and go to the San Ignacio Mapuche community in Neuquén, about sixty kilometres from Junín de los Andes, and are buried in a mound built in the shape of a cultrún, the ceremonial drum. The body that Rome catalogued in a zinc urn in 1924 is put into Mapuche ground under a Mapuche form. Manuel Namuncurá's own grave, somewhere on this same land, is still lost. Only the English account still places the relics on the Colorado.
suggested_refs: The cultrún-shaped burial mound at the San Ignacio community, Neuquén
